title: Abak Atama
author: Iquo Bassey
desc: Palm fruit boiled twenty-five minutes, pounded with light strikes so the nuts do not break, and a litre and a half of water squeezed through the pulp by hand.
longDesc: Abak atama is the Akwa Ibom palm nut soup and the atama leaf is what distinguishes it — shredded very finely and added only once the soup has begun to thicken. The extraction is the work: a big derica cup of palm fruit boils about twenty-five minutes, then is pounded with deliberately light strikes so the nuts are separated from the flesh without being cracked, and a litre and a half of water is squeezed through the pulp by hand and sieved into the pot. Half a piece of uyayak — Aidan fruit — goes in with the pepper and crayfish.
ingredients: 1 medium bunch atama, shredded very finely
steps: Boil the palm fruit about 25 minutes.
Pound it to separate the flesh from the nut, using light strikes so you do not break the nuts.
Pour 1.5 litres of water (about one and a half bottles) over the pounded palm fruit and squeeze the juice from the pulp by hand.
Sieve the liquid into a pot.
Season the beef and steam it until half cooked.
Add the beef to the palm sauce and bring to the boil.
Add the stockfish head, pomo, periwinkle, smoked prawn and smoked fish.
Add the uyayak, dry pepper, crayfish seasoning, beef seasoning and salt.
Cook until the soup begins to thicken, then add the finely shredded atama.
Continue until the soup thickens to the consistency you want.
Serve with pounded yam, rice or eba.
chefTips: Light strikes in the mortar. Cracking the nuts puts palm kernel into the soup, which is a different and wrong-tasting oil.
Atama goes in only once the soup has begun to thicken — not before. It is a strong leaf and it does not need long.
Shred the atama very finely. Whole or roughly torn, it dominates everything.
A litre and a half of water through one big derica cup of palm fruit. Squeeze by hand; a blender cannot do this job.
Half a piece of uyayak, which is Aidan fruit — the same spice the Delta banga recipes use under the same name.
Steam the beef only until half cooked before it goes in. It finishes in the palm sauce.
Periwinkle in the shell. Eating them out of the shell is part of the dish, and they keep their texture better.
commonMistakes: Pounding hard enough to crack the nuts.
Cooking the beef through before it meets the palm sauce.
Trying to extract the cream in a blender.
sources: Adapted from 'How to make Abak Atama Soup', byline '1Qfoodplatter'. Placed as Calabar and Akwa Ibom, and noted as common in 'south east and delta regions of Nigeria', also in Ghana, Cameroon and Côte d'Ivoire. Quantities as printed: 1 big derica cup Palm fruit; 1 medium bunch Atama (shredded very finely); 8 pieces Beef; 8 pieces Pomo; 1 cup Periwinkle (in shell); 4 medium pieces Crab; 1 stock fish head; 1 medium smoked fish; 1/2 cup smoked prawn; 1/2 piece Uyayak; 1 tablespoon dry Pepper; 2 tablets crayfish seasoning; 1 beef seasoning; salt. Yield not specified.

The extraction is as printed: boil the eyop (palm fruit) about 25 minutes; pound to separate flesh from nut with 'light strikes to avoid breaking the nuts'; 'pour 1½ bottles of water (1.5 litres)' into the palm fruit and squeeze the juice from the pulp by hand; sieve into the pot.
Cues as printed: beef steamed 'until half cooked'; 'cook until thickening begins, then add atama'; then 'until soup thickens to the desired consistency'. Serving: pounded yam, rice or eba.

CROSS-REGIONAL NAMING: the Kitchen Butterfly banga page gives the Akwa Ibom and Cross River name for the palm nut soup family as 'Efere Abak/Atama', which matches this dish. The same page gives Banga for Edo, Delta and Urhobo, Ofe Akwu for Igbo, Obe Eyin for Yoruba and Obe-Ekpo for Itsekiri.

ON UYAYAK: Dunni Obata's banga column names it as 'Uyayak (Aidan fruit)' and uses '1 small/medium'. Nigerian Food TV glosses banga spice as 'Aidan fruit+Rohojie'. So the same spice crosses from Akwa Ibom into the Delta soups under the same name.

ON ATAMA, and a wrinkle worth recording: atama is a Cross River and Efik leaf, but it appears in Dunni Obata's Delta banga recipe as 'Atama or bitter leaf (handful)'. Searches for atama outside this region returned only Efik and Ibibio results, so it belongs here rather than in the Middle Belt where it is sometimes listed.
For the palm nut extraction from scratch in more detail, including the disagreement over whether the extraction water should be hot or cold, see NGA043.
healthBenefits: Palm fruit pulp is exceptionally rich in carotenoids and tocotrienols.
Periwinkle and crab are both very lean, high-iron proteins.
Atama is traditionally used as a digestive.
culturalNote: Abak atama belongs to the same palm nut family as banga and ofe akwu, and the thing that makes it Akwa Ibom rather than Delta or Igbo is the atama leaf. Each community in the palm belt has taken the same base and claimed it with a different aromatic — banga spice and the oburunbebe stick in the Delta, scent leaf and ugu in Igboland, atama here.
